translations.title: A Towering Sequence
translations.explanation: Learning goal: create sequences from a context and describe a precise rule for obtaining each term from earlier terms. A sequence is an ordered list: a first term and a rule can define later terms. In a three-peg disc-transfer puzzle, moving n discs optimally requires transferring n-1 smaller discs away, moving the largest disc once, and transferring the smaller stack back. Consequently M(1)=1 and M(n)=2M(n-1)+1. The number of moves depends on the number of discs, not on the physical size of the pegs.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Sequence: ordered terms with positions. Recursive description: state the initial term and how the next term is calculated. With start 2 and next=2*previous-1, the first five terms are 2,3,5,9,17; another initial term gives a different valid sequence. Disc-transfer minimum: M(1)=1, M(n)=2M(n-1)+1, so M(n)=2^n-1 for positive integer n. For the optional two-colour checker exchange puzzle with n checkers of each colour, n(n+2) legal moves are needed under the stated forward and jump restrictions; justify a proposed rule rather than guessing from two cases.
translations.workedExamples: Sequence example: starting with 4 and applying next=2*previous-1 generates 4,7,13,25,49. Recursive disc example: M(2)=3, M(3)=7, M(4)=15, M(5)=31, M(7)=127. Explanation: to move five discs, shift four aside (15), move the bottom disc (1), restore four (15): 31. Fractional recursion: starting at 1/2, repeatedly halve to obtain 1/4,1/8,1/16,1/32,1/64. Backward recursion: if a4=-7 and a(n+1)=-2a(n)+3 then a3=5, a2=-1, a1=2; next terms a5=17,a6=-31,a7=65.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Identify the term position and initial value. 2. Translate the verbal relationship into a recurrence, using parentheses correctly (2x-1 is not 1-2x). 3. Apply the recurrence term-by-term while retaining the order. 4. When a solution demands an explanation, justify why both sub-puzzles of size n-1 are necessary and sufficient. 5. Check the predicted sequence by hand for 1,2,3,4 discs; do not treat an untested pattern as proof.
translations.commonMistakes: Interpreting 'one less than twice the previous term' as 1-2x rather than 2x-1; forgetting to include the initial term in the requested number of terms; using 2^n instead of 2^n-1 for the disc minimum; treating a physical strategy or checker drawing as automatically verified by a numeric response.
translations.quickSummary: An ordered list with a specified first term and recursive rule defines a sequence. The three-peg disc puzzle yields 1,3,7,15,31,... and M(n)=2M(n-1)+1. Explain the move constraints before claiming a minimum. The optional checker task and open explanations are teacher-reviewed.

translations.title: Introducing Geometric Sequences
translations.explanation: Learn to distinguish a geometric sequence by a constant nonzero growth factor between consecutive terms. In a paper-halving context, the number of pieces doubles while the area of each piece halves, yet their product stays constant. Use tables, index-versus-value graphs, and numerical rules rather than treating a continuous curve as the discrete sequence. A growth factor between zero and one describes decay; negative factors alternate signs.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Geometric sequence: a(n+1)=r*a(n), r a constant ratio when a(n) nonzero. Explicit form a(n)=a(0)*r^n for an index starting at zero. For an 8-by-10-inch sheet cut into equal halves n times, pieces P(n)=2^n, area A(n)=80/2^n square inches and P(n)A(n)=80. From adjacent terms, r=a(n+1)/a(n) if denominator not zero; compare consecutive ratios before claiming a sequence is geometric.
translations.workedExamples: Paper cuts: after 5 cuts 32 pieces and 2.5 square inches each; after 6 cuts 64 pieces and 1.25 square inches each, preserving 80 square inches. Missing terms: 1.5, 3, 6, 12, 24, 48 has factor 2; 200,20,2,0.2,0.02,0.002 has factor 0.1. Shrinking pattern 256,192,144,108,81 has factor 3/4. In a fractal-style triangle pattern, the number of retained pieces grows by 3 each step while their individual areas shrink by 4 each step.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Label the input as whole-number steps or cuts. 2. Form a table for two successive terms. 3. Divide new by previous to find the growth factor when defined. 4. Extend terms by multiplying by the same factor. 5. Check units, discrete graph domain and any conserved quantity. 6. Explain a graph or physical cutting task to a teacher rather than assuming a number proves the diagram.
translations.commonMistakes: Confusing growth factor 0.75 with a decrease of 0.75 units. Treating 0.5 times an area as a decrease of 0.5 square inches. Graphing continuous x-values as if a discrete number of cuts could be fractional. Using a single ratio without checking the rest of the sequence.
translations.quickSummary: A geometric sequence has a constant multiplier. Doubling the number of pieces and halving their individual areas preserves the original sheet area. Multipliers above one grow; positive multipliers below one decay. Show a table or graph and justify each model.

translations.title: Different Types of Sequences
translations.explanation: Distinguish arithmetic sequences, which add a fixed common difference, from geometric sequences, which multiply by a fixed common ratio; a sequence may be neither. Read tabular and graphed term data with the correct indices, compare the 10th terms of different growth patterns, and explain how a positive constant sequence can satisfy both rules.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Arithmetic a(n+1)=a(n)+d, a(n)=a(1)+(n-1)d, indexed at 1. Geometric a(n+1)=r*a(n), a(n)=a(1)r^(n-1), for nonzero consecutive terms and constant r. A sequence such as 0,5,15,30,50 grows with differences 5,10,15,20, so it is neither arithmetic nor geometric. For positive constant c,c,c,... the common difference is 0 and the ratio is 1.
translations.workedExamples: Arithmetic A: 30,40,50,60,70 gives A(10)=30+9*10=120. Nonlinear B: 0,5,15,30,50 gives B(n)=5*n*(n-1)/2, B(10)=225. Geometric C: 1,2,4,8,16 gives C(10)=2^9=512. So B, not A, is second largest at term 10. Function warm-up: f(n)=3n-7 yields f(0)=-7, f(3)=2 and f(10)=23. When input intervals vary, repeated output ratios alone do not establish a single ratio between consecutive positions.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Identify each term's actual position. Subtract consecutive terms to test for constant difference; divide consecutive nonzero terms to test for constant ratio. If neither invariant holds, classify 'neither' and find a separate justified rule where possible. For a comparison of 10th terms calculate each from its particular model and compare actual values, not only initial terms.
translations.commonMistakes: Confusing a constant growth difference with a growth ratio; mistaking gaps in graph x-values for consecutive terms; claiming any geometric pattern must rise; treating a constant sequence with positive terms as belonging to only one category.
translations.quickSummary: Arithmetic means constant difference, geometric means constant ratio, and some sequences satisfy neither. Check multiple consecutive pairs and preserve the index domain when reading graphs.

translations.title: Using Technology to Work with Sequences
translations.explanation: Learn how a spreadsheet uses cell references and formula fill-down to generate recursive sequences; use graphing technology to display values at integer positions. Example inputs A1=2,A2=3,A3=-10,A4=0.2 yield B1=A1+A2=5, B2=A3*A4=-2, B3=B1+333=338 and B4=abs(B2)=2. Entering a formula begins with '=', whereas a value or text entry does not recalculate a referenced formula. To generate 10,13,16,... set A1=10 and A2= A1+3, then fill down. For 16,8,4,... use B1=16,B2=B1*0.5. Read ratios and differences in adjacent rows to verify the type.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cell references are addresses. Relative reference A1 in formula =A1+3 changes to A2 when copied down one row. Arithmetic sequence in a sheet: =previous+constant; geometric sequence =previous*constant. For list 700,70,7,.7,.07 use successive quotient =C2/C1 =0.1; for 7,10.5,14,17.5 successive difference =E2-E1 =3.5. Graphing (n,a(n)) plots term number horizontally and value vertically. To ensure plotted points form a function, no input n can pair with two different outputs.
translations.workedExamples: Spreadsheet formula demonstration: B1=2+3=5; B2=-10*0.2=-2; B3=5+333=338; B4=abs(-2)=2. Fill-down examples: initial 12 and +3 yields 12,15,18; initial 12 and -1 yields 12,11,10; initial 10 and factor3 yields 10,30,90. For a table of term indices 0 through9, formula =2*A1+5 in B1 and fill down gives 5,7,9,...,23. The sequence 8,12,18,27,40.5 is geometric factor1.5, while 50,42.1,34.2,26.3 is arithmetic difference-7.9.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: 1. Enter the starting value in the first row. 2. Type an equals sign and a formula that references the previous row. 3. Fill down and check the first three calculated entries by hand. 4. Use adjacent subtraction or quotient columns, taking care not to divide by zero. 5. To graph, put integer term indices into column one and output values into column two. 6. For each graph check whether one input has more than one output and explain why a vertical line is or is not valid.
translations.commonMistakes: Typing A1+3 without '=' and expecting a calculation; copying an absolute address when a relative reference is needed; claiming an arithmetic pattern because all outputs rise, without checking constant differences; drawing a continuous curve for a discrete sequence; treating negative x-values as incorrect when plotting valid second-quadrant points.
translations.quickSummary: Spreadsheet cell references and fill-down generate recurrence terms. Adjacent differences reveal arithmetic sequences, adjacent quotients reveal geometric sequences. A table of ordered pairs can be graphed; a function requires exactly one output for each input.

translations.title: Sequences are Functions
translations.explanation: Learning goals: Comprehend that sequences are functions whose domain is a subset of the integers. Create (in writing) a recursive definition for a sequence using function notation. For a triangular dot pattern with one dot at step 1 and a new row of n dots at step n, the count is D(1)=1 and D(n)=D(n-1)+n for whole-number n>=2. The first five counts are 1,3,6,10,15 and the explicit formula is n(n+1)/2. Its differences increase, so it is neither arithmetic nor geometric. A recursive equation without a starting term is incomplete.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Sequence as function: An integer-indexed function has one output for each permitted input n. Rule: State domain and first term. Example: D: positive integers to nonnegative integers.
Recursive notation: A term is defined through an earlier term. Rule: For n>=2, f(n)=f(n-1)+d, with f(1) specified. Example: f(1)=6, f(n)=f(n-1)+4.
Nonlinear triangular numbers: Each new triangle row adds its row number. Rule: T(n)=T(n-1)+n; T(1)=1. Example: 1,3,6,10,15
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: How many dots are there at step 5? Method: Use the previous count and add the new row. Steps: D(1)=1. D(2)=1+2=3; D(3)=3+3=6. D(4)=6+4=10; D(5)=10+5=15. Answer: 15 dots Check: Differences 2,3,4,5 increase, not a constant.
Example 2: Classify 30,40,50,... and 1,3,7,15,... Method: Check consecutive differences and ratios. Steps: The first has constant +10, hence arithmetic. The second has differences 2,4,8 so not arithmetic. Ratios 3,7/3,15/7 differ so not geometric. Answer: The first is arithmetic; second is neither. Check: 1,3,7,15 follows next=2*previous+1.

translations.title: Representing Sequences
translations.explanation: Learning goals: Create a table, graph, or recursive definition of a sequence from given information. A sequence can be represented as indexed terms, an input-output table, discrete graph points or a recurrence. For 5,15,25,35,45 the common difference is 10. For g(1)=-5 and g(n)=-2g(n-1), the first four terms are -5,10,-20,40. A geometric list of -factor values alternates signs. For the growing square arrangement with totals 1,5,14,... each new step adds n^2, so S(1)=1 and S(n)=S(n-1)+n^2; S(4)=30. For maximal planar pieces from n straight cuts, R(n)=1+n(n+1)/2.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Four representations: One indexed sequence can appear as numbers, table, graph and recurrence. Rule: Keep index and start conditions consistent. Example: 4,7,10,13 has f(1)=4, f(n)=f(n-1)+3.
Sign-changing geometric sequence: Negative ratio reverses the sign every step. Rule: g(n)=-2g(n-1). Example: -5,10,-20,40.
Sum of squares pattern: A new n-by-n block contributes n squared cells. Rule: S(n)=S(n-1)+n^2. Example: S(1)=1, S(2)=5, S(3)=14, S(4)=30.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: A pattern totals 1,5,14 squares at steps 1,2,3. What is step 4? Method: Add a new 4-by-4 block. Steps: The added counts are 1,4,9 at the first three steps. Step 4 adds 16. S(4)=14+16=30. Answer: 30 squares Check: The differences 4,9,16 are not constant.
Example 2: Starting with one region, how many at most after four straight cuts? Method: Each new line can cross all previous lines at distinct points. Steps: New regions after cuts 1,2,3,4 are 1,2,3,4. Total is 1+1+2+3+4=11. Answer: 11 regions Check: A drawing must actually exhibit the maximal intersections.

translations.title: Representing More Sequences
translations.explanation: Learning goals: Determine what information is needed to represent a sequence in different ways. Ask questions to elicit information. A recursive rule alone may not identify a unique sequence: f(n)=f(n-1)-5 requires a starting term. A defined function also needs a meaningful index domain. In a two-person information gap, request the missing first term, multiplier or difference and index origin, then justify the derived table/graph. For H(1)=20.25 with common ratio 2/3, the first terms are 20.25,13.5,9,6. A visual pattern with count n^2+3n+3 starting at n=0 has counts 3,7,13,21,...; differences 4,6,8 increase.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Missing initial condition: A recurrence does not specify its first value without an initial term. Rule: Ask for f(1) or f(0) explicitly. Example: f(n)=f(n-1)-5 admits many sequences.
Questioning for information: Mathematical information can be shared and justified through precise questions. Rule: Request the start index, initial term and update relationship. Example: Given H(1)=20.25 and ratio 2/3, H(3)=9.
Quadratic visual count: A pattern with n^2+3n+3 increases by nonconstant amounts. Rule: At n=0 count=3; n=1 count=7. Example: 3,7,13,21
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: Given H(1)=20.25 and factor 2/3, find H(4). Method: Multiply by the common ratio three times. Steps: H(2)=13.5. H(3)=9. H(4)=6. Answer: 6 Check: H(1)=(81/4), H(4)=(81/4)*(8/27)=6.
Example 2: For D(n)=n^2+3n+3 from step zero, find the first four values. Method: Evaluate the expression for whole-number inputs. Steps: D(0)=3. D(1)=7; D(2)=13. D(3)=21. Answer: 3,7,13,21 Check: Differences 4,6,8 are nonconstant.

translations.title: The $n^{\text{th}}$ Term
translations.explanation: Learning goals: Interpret an equation for the $n^{\text{th}}$ term of a sequence. Justify (orally and in writing) why different equations can represent the same sequence. The recursive form f(n)=2f(n-1) with f(1)=3 has explicit form f(n)=3*2^(n-1) for integers n>=1. The same function can be written as (3/2)*2^n on the same domain. In repeated paper slicing, 80 square inches reduced to one fourth of the previous piece per stage yields A(1)=80 and A(n)=80*(1/4)^(n-1). Using exponents avoids iterating through every earlier value, but the stated domain is constrained by the physical model.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Explicit term rule: A formula for term n uses n without earlier terms. Rule: g(n)=g(1)*r^(n-1). Example: g(1)=3,r=2 yields 3*2^(n-1).
Equivalent expressions: Algebraically different formulas can define equal values. Rule: 3*2^(n-1)=(3/2)*2^n. Example: At n=4 both are 24.
Domain matters: Sequence indices are positive or nonnegative integers according to the model. Rule: Do not interpolate a fractional number of cuts. Example: 1,2,3,... rather than all real n.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: f(1)=3, f(n)=2f(n-1). Find f(6). Method: Apply the exponent formula. Steps: f(n)=3*2^(n-1). f(6)=3*2^5. 3*32=96. Answer: 96 Check: Term 1 gives 3, not 6.
Example 2: A(1)=80 and each new piece has one-quarter the area. Find A(4). Method: Compute 80*(1/4)^3. Steps: There are three multiplications by 1/4. A(4)=80/64. Answer: 5/4 square inches Check: Physical model requires a feasible step count.

translations.title: Adding Up
translations.explanation: Learning goals: Calculate the sum of a simple geometric sequence describing a situation without the use of a formula. A sequence sum adds its terms; it is not another single term. For 1,2,4,8,16,32,64 the seven-term sum is 127, despite last term 64. For half the remainder at each stop, the covered fractions after two and four stops are 3/4 and 15/16; no finite number of stops reaches 1 exactly. For a triangular design whose sides are quadrupled at each step, S(0)=3, S(n)=3*4^n, while newly added triangles can follow a separate geometric sequence. translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Finite sequence sum: Add exactly the specified terms. Rule: S_N = a1+a2+...+aN. Example: 1+2+4+8=15.
Geometric fractions: Repeatedly halve a remaining positive quantity. Rule: Covered proportion after n halves: 1-(1/2)^n. Example: After four stops: 15/16.
Fractal geometric growth: Counts and areas must be tracked separately. Rule: Initial 3 edges quadruple at each new subdivision step. Example: 3,12,48 sides at steps 0,1,2.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: How much is received if daily receipts double from 1 through seven days? Method: List terms and add. Steps: Terms are 1,2,4,8,16,32,64. Sum first four:15; last three:112. Total 127. Answer: 127 Check: A sum is not the final 64.
Example 2: After four halfway segments, what fraction of a hallway has been covered? Method: Subtract remaining fraction from one. Steps: Remaining = (1/2)^4=1/16. Covered=1-1/16. Answer: 15/16 Check: No finite n covers all of it under exact halving.

translations.title: Combining Functions
translations.explanation:
This lesson combines two functions at the same input through arithmetic: (f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x), (f−g)(x)=f(x)−g(x), (fg)(x)=f(x)g(x), and (f/g)(x)=f(x)/g(x) where g(x)≠0. Graphs and tables allow function values to be combined without explicit formulas. In the publisher context, annual books sold per person is total annual books sold divided by the population: both are measured in millions, so their ratio has units of books per person. Combining by arithmetic is distinct from composition f(g(x)), which substitutes an output into a second function and is not the central focus of this lesson.

Edulytics original standards extension (HSF-BF.A.1.c; not attributed to the source publisher): composition builds a new function by using the output of an inner function as the input of an outer function. For two functions f and g, the composition f(g(x)) generally differs from both the product f(x)g(x) and the reverse composition g(f(x)). In a real context, the inner function’s output units must match the outer function’s input units.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
At the same input x: (f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x); (f−g)(x)=f(x)−g(x); (fg)(x)=f(x)g(x); (f/g)(x)=f(x)/g(x), with g(x)≠0. Domains of sums, differences and products are the intersection of the original domains; quotient domains also exclude zeros of the divisor. Interpret the units of each combined quantity, not just its numerical value. For a combined graph, read f(x) and g(x) at the SAME x before adding or otherwise combining their y-values. Composition f(g(x)) is a separate operation and should not be confused with the product fg.

Edulytics extension — composition: (f∘g)(x)=f(g(x)). Evaluate g first, then apply f. The composition domain consists of x in the domain of g for which g(x) lies in the domain of f. Do not substitute outputs from different x values or confuse f(g(x)) with (fg)(x). Composition is generally not commutative: f∘g need not equal g∘f. Units must chain: minutes→height in meters→temperature in degrees Celsius.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1 (books per person): In 2010, 2,530 million books were sold in the U.S. and the U.S. population was 309.35 million. Let B(0)=2,530 and P(0)=309.35. Then R(0)=B(0)/P(0)=2,530/309.35≈8.178 books per person. The millions cancel. R(0) is not the total book sales or the number of people. Example 2 (function arithmetic): Let f(x)=2x+3 and g(x)=x−1. Their sum is (f+g)(x)=3x+2, so (f+g)(4)=14. Their product is (fg)(x)=(2x+3)(x−1)=2x²+x−3. Their quotient is (f/g)(x)=(2x+3)/(x−1), defined only when x≠1; at x=4, its value is 11/3. Example 3 (graph table): If f(2)=5 and g(2)=−3, the combined graph for h=f+g contains (2,2), while the graph of f−g contains (2,8); add outputs at a shared input.

Edulytics extension, Example 4 — algebraic composition: f(x)=2x+1 and g(x)=3x−4. Then f(g(x))=2(3x−4)+1=6x−7, while g(f(x))=3(2x+1)−4=6x−1. At x=2, f(g(2))=5, but g(f(2))=11. This demonstrates why composition is not simply multiplication and its order matters. Example 5 — temperature of a weather balloon: its height in meters after t minutes is h(t)=1,000+2t; atmospheric temperature in degrees Celsius at height y meters is T(y)=20−0.006y. Their composition is T(h(t))=20−0.006(1,000+2t)=14−0.012t °C. At t=5 minutes, the predicted temperature is 13.94°C. The input/output units match: time→height→temperature.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
1. Identify the two functions and the desired operation (sum, difference, product or quotient). 2. Determine the common domain; for a quotient also exclude inputs where g(x)=0. 3. If expressions are supplied, combine them algebraically and simplify carefully. 4. If a graph/table is supplied, read both outputs at the same x and carry out the operation. 5. When combining real-world quantities, state the output units and interpret the result. 6. Check a sample input with both the original and simplified formulas, and validate any denominator restrictions.

Edulytics extension for HSF-BF.A.1.c: 1. Identify the outer function f and the inner function g. 2. Evaluate or simplify g(x) first. 3. Replace the input of f with the entire expression g(x), keeping parentheses. 4. Simplify f(g(x)) without changing the order. 5. Check the domain: g(x) must be defined and its value must be an allowed input to f. 6. In contexts, verify output-input units are compatible across functions. 7. Test a numeric value using separate inner and outer evaluations to confirm the formula.
translations.commonMistakes:
Do not combine inputs instead of outputs. For a quotient, exclude denominator zeros even if algebraic cancellation occurs. Do not mistake composition f(g(x)) for the product (fg)(x). Do not assume book sales and population have the same output unit just because both are measured in millions: their ratio is books per person.

Edulytics extension: (f∘g)(x) is not f(x)g(x); it is f(g(x)). In general g(f(x)) differs from f(g(x)). A physically invalid height or a mismatched output unit makes a contextual composition meaningless. Domain restrictions propagate through the inner-to-outer calculation.
translations.quickSummary:
At each permitted x, combine f(x) and g(x) by arithmetic. For division, require g(x)≠0 and interpret units. Book sales divided by population yields books per person. Composition f(g(x)) is a different skill.

Edulytics extension: build compositions by substituting the inner output into the outer function. Example f(g(x))=6x−7 and g(f(x))=6x−1 for f(x)=2x+1, g(x)=3x−4. This extension is original Edulytics content beyond the publisher lesson’s arithmetic focus.
